A contractor whose client asked them to install the Drata agent for SOC 2 said they don't like running an agent on their machine at all. Their plan was to ignore the request and hope it went away, with quitting as the most appealing fallback.

The contractor said the Drata agent requirement "comes from the sales people. They want to provide a 'SOC 2 Audited' certificate to their potential customers. They don't give a rats ass about actual security," and doubted the requirement adds much real security.

Ignoring the request won't work, one commenter said: if you're in the corporate directory, you show up as noncompliant in the Drata dashboard. They called such agents "extremely normal on company hardware." Their advice: don't run multiple clients on personal hardware; take a company laptop or lease a dedicated one and bill the client.

Workarounds the contractor considered for isolating the Drata agent: run it in a VM, use an old laptop with the wi-fi card removed, buy a dedicated machine, or put it on a VLAN routed to a VPN. The client was willing to pay for a new laptop. Others noted agent software can easily detect a VM, though QEMU can mask it.
